title: Frizzled's Second Job: Aligning a Sheet

scenes.visual: Top-down cartoon of a translucent fruit-fly wing filling 70% of the frame, covered with tiny emerald hairs pointing uniformly from left (wing base) toward right (wing tip). A gentle wave of light sweeps along the aligned hairs. High-contrast title fades cleanly above the wing: 'Frizzled's Second Job: Aligning a Sheet'.

scenes.tts: In the first film, Frizzled and Dishevelled helped Wint save beta-catenin from destruction. How can those same two proteins align every hair on a fly wing without beta-catenin? They run a separate polarity system.
scenes.caption: In the first film, Frizzled and Dishevelled helped Wnt save β-catenin from destruction. How can those same two proteins align every hair on a fly wing without β-catenin? They run a separate polarity system.
scenes.visual: Upper-left corner briefly shows a dimmed badge of teal 'Frizzled' and amber 'Dishevelled' (matching the first film's colours), then zooms smoothly into the fly-wing epithelium: a honeycomb sheet of hexagonal cells ('schematic'), each sprouting one emerald hair pointing right ('Wing tip ->').
scenes.narration: In the first film, Frizzled and Dishevelled helped Wnt save β-catenin from destruction. How can those same two proteins align every hair on a fly wing without β-catenin? They run a separate polarity system.

scenes.tts: Look closely at this sheet of fly wing cells. Every cell grows one emerald hair, and every hair points toward the wing tip. This shared direction across the plane of a sheet is planar cell polarity. Yet no single cell can see the whole wing.
scenes.caption: Look closely at this sheet of fly wing cells. Every cell grows one emerald hair, and every hair points toward the wing tip. This shared direction across the plane of a sheet is planar cell polarity. Yet no single cell can see the whole wing.
scenes.visual: Camera pans gently across the carried hexagonal sheet ('schematic'). One cell lights up with a tight glowing ring around its immediate six neighbours ('Local view only'), showing it touches only the cells beside it while the distant wing tip sits far off to the right. Top label: 'Planar cell polarity'.
scenes.narration: Look closely at this sheet of fly wing cells. Every cell grows one emerald hair, and every hair points toward the wing tip. This shared direction across the plane of a sheet is planar cell polarity. Yet no single cell can see the whole wing.

scenes.tts: To test how cells learn direction, Charles Vinson and Paul Adler made small patches lacking Frizzled inside normal wings. Then they looked closely at the normal cells beside each patch.
scenes.caption: To test how cells learn direction, Charles Vinson and Paul Adler made small patches lacking Frizzled inside normal wings. Then they looked closely at the normal cells beside each patch.
scenes.visual: In the centre of the normal hexagonal sheet, a five-cell cluster turns dark outline-only ('No Frizzled'; corner note 'Vinson & Adler, 1987'). Hairs inside the mutant patch spin into disordered directions. Normal cells directly to the left ('Body side') and right ('Tip side') of the patch gain a soft highlight ring as the camera eases in on them.
scenes.narration: To test how cells learn direction, Charles Vinson and Paul Adler made small patches lacking Frizzled inside normal wings. Then they looked closely at the normal cells beside each patch.

scenes.tts: Normal hairs next to the patch point toward it. On the tip side, that means pointing backward, the wrong way. On the body side, toward the patch is still toward the tip. Because genetically normal cells changed direction, cells must pass polarity information from neighbour to neighbour across the sheet.
scenes.caption: Normal hairs next to the patch point toward it. On the tip side, that means pointing backward, the wrong way. On the body side, toward the patch is still toward the tip. Because genetically normal cells changed direction, cells must pass polarity information from neighbour to neighbour across the sheet.
scenes.visual: On the right ('Tip side'), emerald hairs on normal cells smoothly rotate backward toward the patch and turn bright coral-orange to mark misdirection ('Tip side: misdirected'). On the left ('Body side'), emerald hairs stay aligned rightward ('Body side: normal'). Subtle curved arrows pulse across cell borders ('Neighbour-to-neighbour cue'). Empathy fix: Add small arrows on both sides of the patch, all aimed at it; tip-side arrows are highlighted as 'backward'.
scenes.narration: Normal hairs next to the patch point toward it. On the tip side, that means pointing backward, the wrong way. On the body side, toward the patch is still toward the tip. Because genetically normal cells changed direction, cells must pass polarity information from neighbour to neighbour across the sheet.

scenes.tts: Zoom into normal wing cells to see how each cell tells its two sides apart. Teal Frizzled and amber Dishevelled gather along the tip-side edge of every cell. On the opposite edge, magenta Van Gogh gathers with its lavender partner, Prickle. Each cell builds two distinct sides.
scenes.caption: Zoom into normal wing cells to see how each cell tells its two sides apart. Teal Frizzled and amber Dishevelled gather along the tip-side edge of every cell. On the opposite edge, magenta Van Gogh gathers with its lavender partner, Prickle. Each cell builds two distinct sides.
scenes.visual: The mutant patch heals back into a zoomed-in row of six normal hexagonal wing cells filling 65% of frame height ('schematic'). Inside every cell, teal 'Frizzled' and amber 'Dishevelled' particles (same colours as the first film) drift smoothly to the right-hand ('Tip-side') edge, while magenta 'Van Gogh' and lavender 'Prickle' drift to the left-hand ('Body-side') edge.
scenes.narration: Zoom into normal wing cells to see how each cell tells its two sides apart. Teal Frizzled and amber Dishevelled gather along the tip-side edge of every cell. On the opposite edge, magenta Van Gogh gathers with its lavender partner, Prickle. Each cell builds two distinct sides.

scenes.tts: Across every shared border, silver Flamingo bridges one cell's Frizzled edge to its neighbour's Van Gogh edge. Each cell grows its actin hair right at its Frizzled edge, so every hair points together.
scenes.caption: Across every shared border, silver Flamingo bridges one cell's Frizzled edge to its neighbour's Van Gogh edge. Each cell grows its actin hair right at its Frizzled edge, so every hair points together.
scenes.visual: Bright silver-white 'Flamingo' cadherin bridges snap across every cell border, locking each cell's teal 'Frizzled' edge face-to-face with the next cell's magenta 'Van Gogh' edge. From every teal edge, an emerald actin bundle sprouts and extends rightward into a sharp wing hair. Empathy fix: Label each border bridge 'Frizzled : Van Gogh'.
scenes.narration: Across every shared border, silver Flamingo bridges one cell's Frizzled edge to its neighbour's Van Gogh edge. Each cell grows its actin hair right at its Frizzled edge, so every hair points together.

scenes.tts: Notice what is absent from this entire picture. Planar polarity in the wing uses no beta-catenin and no TCF. Instead of switching on TCF genes, Frizzled and Dishevelled set the place where each cell builds its hair.
scenes.caption: Notice what is absent from this entire picture. Planar polarity in the wing uses no β-catenin and no TCF. Instead of switching on TCF genes, Frizzled and Dishevelled set the place where each cell builds its hair.
scenes.visual: A faint nucleus outline inside each wing cell stays dim and quiet (label: 'No β-catenin'), while the bright teal-against-magenta cell edges and emerald actin hairs pulse cleanly to highlight local edge organization.
scenes.narration: Notice what is absent from this entire picture. Planar polarity in the wing uses no β-catenin and no TCF. Instead of switching on TCF genes, Frizzled and Dishevelled set the place where each cell builds its hair.

scenes.tts: Vertebrates reuse these same polarity genes to shape early tissues. The future brain and spinal cord begin as a flat sheet called the neural plate. Guided by polarity proteins and Wint signals, cells identify which edge faces the midline. They squeeze between neighbours to narrow the plate and fold it into a tube.
scenes.caption: Vertebrates reuse these same polarity genes to shape early tissues. The future brain and spinal cord begin as a flat sheet called the neural plate. Guided by polarity proteins and Wnt signals, cells identify which edge faces the midline. They squeeze between neighbours to narrow the plate and fold it into a tube.
scenes.visual: The carried hexagonal sheet smoothly widens into a top-down vertebrate 'Neural plate' ('schematic') with a dashed central 'Midline'. Teal ('Frizzled') and magenta ('Vangl') edges align relative to the midline as faint gold 'Wnt' dots drift nearby. Cells intercalate smoothly inward between neighbours, narrowing the sheet horizontally and lengthening it vertically while its outer folds curl up toward each other.
scenes.narration: Vertebrates reuse these same polarity genes to shape early tissues. The future brain and spinal cord begin as a flat sheet called the neural plate. Guided by polarity proteins and Wnt signals, cells identify which edge faces the midline. They squeeze between neighbours to narrow the plate and fold it into a tube.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Suppose these cells could not tell which edge faces the midline. What would happen to the plate's width, and could its edges still meet?
scenes.caption: Pause and predict. Suppose these cells could not tell which edge faces the midline. What would happen to the plate's width, and could its edges still meet?
scenes.visual: The neural plate rewinds to its flat, wide starting shape ('schematic'). Inside every cell the teal and magenta edge marks fade to grey, so no cell shows which side faces the dashed 'Midline'. A question banner reads: 'Cells cannot find the midline: plate width? Do the folds meet?'
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Suppose these cells could not tell which edge faces the midline. What would happen to the plate's width, and could its edges still meet?

scenes.visual: Hold the wide, grey-edged neural plate and the question banner for 4.5 seconds while the cells jiggle slightly in place and a quiet radial countdown ring completes one smooth turn.

scenes.tts: When planar polarity breaks, cells lose their bearings, and the neural plate can stay too wide to close. Disrupting these genes causes neural tube closure defects, including spina bifida. Whether aligning wing hairs or closing a tube, neighbours sort Frizzled to one edge so the sheet agrees.
scenes.caption: When planar polarity breaks, cells lose their bearings, and the neural plate can stay too wide to close. Disrupting these genes causes neural tube closure defects, including spina bifida. Whether aligning wing hairs or closing a tube, neighbours sort Frizzled to one edge so the sheet agrees.
scenes.visual: Split comparison on the carried neural plate ('schematic'): left side stays narrow and neatly closed ('Normal PCP'); right side shows scrambled teal and magenta edges, cells failing to narrow, and neural folds remaining apart ('Disrupted PCP: open tube').
scenes.narration: When planar polarity breaks, cells lose their bearings, and the neural plate can stay too wide to close. Disrupting these genes causes neural tube closure defects, including spina bifida. Whether aligning wing hairs or closing a tube, neighbours sort Frizzled to one edge so the sheet agrees.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card showing one centered high-contrast line only (no subtitle or smaller line underneath): 'Planar polarity aligns cells as neighbours sort Frizzled to one edge.'
